entries.78daed9cbf75fd49a1590288e6a9ea5956a01d75: <div sID="gen11384" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="53" osisID="Ps.53" sID="Ps.53"/> <div eID="gen11384" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11385" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen11386" type="x-p"/> God speaks once, yea, twice, and it were well if man would even then perceive it; God, in this psalm, speaks twice, for this is the same almost verbatim with the fourteenth psalm. The scope of it is to convince us of our sins, to set us a blushing and trembling because of them; and this is what we are with so much difficulty brought to that there is need of line upon line to this purport. The word, as a convincing word, is compared to a hammer, the strokes whereof must be frequently repeated. God, by the psalmist here, I. Shows us how bad we are, <reference osisRef="Ps.53.1">ver. 1</reference>. II. Proves it upon us by his own certain knowledge, <reference osisRef="Ps.53.2-Ps.53.3">ver. 2, 3</reference>. III. He speaks terror to persecutors, the worst of sinners, <reference osisRef="Ps.53.4-Ps.53.5">ver. 4, 5</reference>. IV. He speaks encouragement to God's persecuted people, <reference osisRef="Ps.53.6">ver. 6</reference>. Some little variation there is between <reference osisRef="Ps.14.1-Ps.14.7">Ps. 14</reference> and <reference osisRef="Ps.53.1-Ps.53.6">this</reference>, but none considerable, only between <reference osisRef="Ps.14.5-Ps.14.6 Ps.53.5">ver. 5</reference> here; some expressions there used are here left out, concerning the shame which the wicked put upon God's people, and instead of that, is here foretold the shame which God would put upon the wicked, which alteration, with some others, he made by divine direction when he delivered it the second time to the chief musician. In singing it we ought to lament the corruption of the human nature, and the wretched degeneracy of the world we live in, yet rejoicing in hope of the great salvation.
entries.f715d18f085b83d92ba5600f30ce4916300df202: <div eID="gen11386" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen11385" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">Human Depravity.</title> <div sID="gen11387" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> The fool hath said in his heart, <hi type="italic">There is</hi> no God. Corrupt are they, and have done abominable iniquity: <hi type="italic">there is</hi> none that doeth good. <hi type="super">2</hi> God looked down from heaven upon the children of men, to see if there were <hi type="italic">any</hi> that did understand, that did seek God. <hi type="super">3</hi> Every one of them is gone back: they are altogether become filthy; <hi type="italic">there is</hi> none that doeth good, no, not one. <hi type="super">4</hi> Have the workers of iniquity no knowledge? who eat up my people <hi type="italic">as</hi> they eat bread: they have not called upon God. <hi type="super">5</hi> There were they in great fear, <hi type="italic">where</hi> no fear was: for God hath scattered the bones of him that encampeth <hi type="italic">against</hi> thee: thou hast put <hi type="italic">them</hi> to shame, because God hath despised them. <hi type="super">6</hi> Oh that the salvation of Israel <hi type="italic">were come</hi> out of Zion! When God bringeth back the captivity of his people, Jacob shall rejoice, <hi type="italic">and</hi> Israel shall be glad. <div eID="gen11387" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11388" type="x-p"/> This psalm was opened before, and therefore we shall here only observe, in short, some things concerning sin, in order to the increasing of our sorrow for it and hatred of it. 1. The fact of sin. Is that proved? Can the charge be made out? Yes, God is a witness to it, an unexceptionable witness: from the place of his holiness he looks on the children of men, and sees how little good there is among them, <reference osisRef="Ps.53.2">v. 2</reference>. All the sinfulness of their hearts and lives in naked and open before him. 2. The fault of sin. Is there any harm in it? Yes, it is iniquity (<reference osisRef="Ps.53.1">v. 1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.53.4">4</reference>); it is an unrighteous thing; it is that which there is no good in (<reference osisRef="Ps.53.1">v. 1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.53.3">3</reference>); it is an evil thing; it is the worst of evils; it is that which makes this world such an evil world as it is; it is going back from God, <reference osisRef="Ps.53.3">v. 3</reference>. 3. The fountain of sin. How comes it that men are so bad? Surely it is because <hi type="italic">there is no fear of God before their eyes:</hi> they <hi type="italic">say in their hearts, "There is no God</hi> at all to call us to an account, none that we need to stand in awe of." Men's bad practices flow from their bad principles; if they profess to know God, yet in works, because in thoughts, they deny him. 4. The folly of sin. He is a fool (in the account of God, whose judgment we are sure is right) that harbours such corrupt thoughts. Atheists, whether in opinion or practice, are the greatest fools in the world. Those that do not seek God do not understand; they are like brute-beasts that have no understanding; for man is distinguished from the brutes, not so much by the powers of reason as by a capacity for religion. <hi type="italic">The workers of iniquity,</hi> whatever they pretend to, <hi type="italic">have no knowledge;</hi> those may truly be said to know nothing that do not know God, <reference osisRef="Ps.53.4">v. 4</reference>. 5. The filthiness of sin. Sinners are corrupt (<reference osisRef="Ps.53.1">v. 1</reference>); their nature is vitiated and spoiled, and the more noble the nature is the more vile it is when it is depraved, as that of the angels. <hi type="italic">Corruptio optimi est pessima—The best things, when corrupted, become the worst.</hi> Their iniquity is abominable; it is odious to the holy God, and it renders them so; whereas otherwise he <hi type="italic">hates nothing that he has made.</hi> It makes men filthy, altogether filthy. Wilful sinners are offensive in the nostrils of the God of heaven and of the holy angels. What decency soever proud sinners pretend to, it is certain that wickedness is the greatest defilement in the world. 6. The fruit of sin. See to what a degree of barbarity it brings men at last; when men's hearts are hardened through the deceitfulness of sin see their cruelty to their brethren, that are bone of their bone—because they will not <hi type="italic">run with them to the same excess of riot,</hi> they <hi type="italic">eat them up as they eat bread;</hi> as if they had not only become beasts, but beasts of prey. And see their contempt of God at the same time. <hi type="italic">They have not called upon</hi> him, but scorn to be beholden to him. 7. The fear and shame that attend sin (<reference osisRef="Ps.53.5">v. 5</reference>): <hi type="italic">There were those in great fear</hi> who had made God their enemy; their own guilty consciences frightened them, and filled them with horror, though otherwise there was no apparent cause of fear. <hi type="italic">The wicked flees when none pursues.</hi> See the ground of this fear; it is because God has formerly <hi type="italic">scattered the bones of those that encamped against</hi> his people, not only broken their power and dispersed their forces, but slain them, and reduced their bodies to dry bones, like those <hi type="italic">scattered at the grave's mouth,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.141.7">Ps. cxli. 7</reference>. Such will be the fate of those that lay siege to the <hi type="italic">camp of the saints and the beloved city,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rev.20.9">Rev. xx. 9</reference>. The apprehensions of this cannot but put those into frights that eat up God's people. This enables the virgin, the daughter of Zion, to put them to shame, and expose them, <hi type="italic">because God has despised them,</hi> to laugh at them, because he that sits in heaven laughs at them. We need not look upon those enemies with fear whom God looks upon with contempt. If he despises them, we may. 8. The faith of the saints, and their hope and power touching the cure of this great evil, <reference osisRef="Ps.53.6">v. 6</reference>. There will come a Saviour, a great salvation, a salvation from sin. Oh that it might be hastened! for it will bring in glorious and joyful times. There were those in the Old-Testament times that looked and hoped, that prayed and waited, for this redemption. (1.) God will, in due time, save his church from the sinful malice of its enemies, which will bring joy to Jacob and Israel, that have long been in a mournful melancholy state. Such salvations were often wrought, and all typical of the everlasting triumphs of the glorious church. (2.) He will save all believers from their own iniquities, that they may not be led captive by them, which will be everlasting matter of joy to them. From this work the Redeemer had his name—<hi type="italic">Jesus,</hi> for <hi type="italic">he shall save his people from their sins,</hi> <reference osisRef="Matt.1.21">Matt. i. 21</reference>.  <chapter eID="Ps.53"/> <div eID="gen11388" type="x-p"/>

entries.cf583350ba6049f92df59594cbfb529ae4fca440: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6078"/><title type="x-s2">PSALM 53</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Ps.53.1-Ps.53.6">Psa 53:1-6</reference>. Upon Mahalath--(See on <reference osisRef="Ps.88.1">Psa 88:1</reference>, title). Why this repetition of the fourteenth Psalm is given we do not know.</title> <div sID="gen9286" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6078"/>1-4. with few verbal changes, correspond with <reference osisRef="Ps.14.1-Ps.14.4">Psa 14:1-4</reference>. <div eID="gen9286" type="x-p"/>
entries.88efe49a9012c17631873c47b8473a87355d9478: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6079"/><div sID="gen9287" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6079"/>5. Instead of assurances of God's presence with the pious, and a complaint of the wicked, <reference osisRef="Ps.14.5">Psa 14:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.14.6">6</reference> portrays the ruin of the latter, whose "bones" even "are scattered" (compare <reference osisRef="Ps.141.7">Psa 141:7</reference>), and who are put to shame as contemptuously rejected of God. <chapter eID="Ps.53"/>

entries.a54f396d17820be16657cf79b33f044369944e27: <div eID="gen20312" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen20313" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen20314" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen20314" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen20313" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen20315" type="x-p"/> The sentiments of atheists and deists, who deny Divine Providence; their character: they are corrupt, foolish, abominable, and cruel, <reference osisRef="Psa.53.1-Psa.53.4">Psa 53:1-4</reference>; God fills them with terror, <reference osisRef="Psa.53.5">Psa 53:5</reference>; reproaches these for their oppression of the poor, <reference osisRef="Psa.53.5">Psa 53:5</reference>. The psalmist prays for the restoration of Israel, <reference osisRef="Psa.53.6">Psa 53:6</reference>. <div eID="gen20315" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20316" type="x-p"/> The title, To the chief Musician upon Mahalath, an instructive Psalm of David. The word מחלת machalath, some translate the president; others, the master or leader of the dance; others, hollow instruments; others, the chorus. A flute pipe, or wind instrument with holes, appears to be what is intended. "To the chief player on the flute;" or, "To the master of the band of pipers." <div eID="gen20316" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20317" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen20317" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20318" type="x-p"/> The fool hath said in his heart - The whole of this Psalm, except a few inconsiderable differences, is the same as the fourteenth; and, therefore, the same notes and analysis may be applied to it; or, by referring to the fourteenth, the reader will find the subject of it amply explained. I shall add a few short notes. <div eID="gen20318" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20319" type="x-p"/> Have done abominable iniquity - Instead of עול avel, evil or iniquity, eight of Kennicott's and De Rossi's MSS. have עלילה alilah, work, which is nearly the same as in Psa xiv.
entries.2f8723479153fbd7579923f52eb71e4a3f20e68b: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen20319" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20320" type="x-p"/> Have the workers of iniquity - For פעלי, poaley, workers seventy-two of Kennicott's and De Rossi's MSS., with several ancient editions, the Chaldee, though not noticed in the Latin translation in the London Polyglot, the Syriac, Vulgate, Septuagint, Ethiopic, and the Arabic, with the Anglo-Saxon, add the word כל col, all, - All the workers of iniquity; which is the reading in the parallel place in <reference osisRef="Psa.14.1-Psa.14.7">Psa 14:1-7</reference> : It may be necessary to observe, that the Chaldee, in the Antwerp and Paris Polyglots, and in that of Justinianus, has not the word כל col, All. <div eID="gen20320" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20321" type="x-p"/> Have not Called upon God - אלהים Elohim; but many MSS. have יהוה Jehovah, Lord.
entries.4ff9980a077f75b552346deeb6501f00f2f93b1f: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen20321" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20322" type="x-p"/> For God hath scattered the bones of him that encampeth against thee: thou hast put them to shame, because God hath despised them - The reader will see, on comparing this with the fifth and sixth verses of <reference osisRef="Psa.14.1-Psa.14.7">Psa 14:1-7</reference>, that the words above are mostly added here to what is said there; and appear to be levelled against the Babylonians, who sacked and ruined Jerusalem, and who were now sacked and ruined in their turn. The sixth verse of <reference osisRef="Psa.14.1-Psa.14.7">Psa 14:1-7</reference>, "Ye have shamed the counsel of the poor, because the Lord is his refuge," is added here by more than twenty of Kennicott's and De Rossi's MSS.
entries.67cc2a13d64892b50e4bb7d4e44f655088272bc6: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen20322" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20323" type="x-p"/> O that the salvation of Israel were come out of Zion! - I have already shown that the proper translation is, "Who shall give from Zion salvation to Israel?" The word salvation is in the plural here, deliverances: but many MSS., with the Septuagint, Vulgate, Arabic, and Anglo-Saxon, have it in the singular. <div eID="gen20323" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20324" type="x-p"/> When God brinyeth back - When Jehovah bringeth back, is the reading of more than twenty of Kennicott's and De Rossi's MSS., with the Septuagint, Syriac, and Chaldee, and Justinianus' Polyglot Psalter. <div eID="gen20324" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20325" type="x-p"/> For larger notes and an analysis, the reader is requested to refer to <reference osisRef="Psa.14.1-Psa.14.7">Psa 14:1-7</reference>; and for a comparison of the two Psalms he may consult Dr. Kennicott's Hebrew Bible, where, under <reference osisRef="Psa.14.1-Psa.14.7">Psa 14:1-7</reference>, in the lower margin, the variations are exhibited at one view.  <chapter eID="Ps.53"/> <div eID="gen20325" type="x-p"/>

entries.2984f2e8b14b575bd38a4d1017ea7b885e29d87e: <reference osisRef="Ps.53.1">Psa 53:1</reference> <div eID="gen9542" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9543" type="x-p"/> The well-grounded asyndeton השׁהיתוּ התעיבוּ is here dismissed; and the expression is rendered more bombastic by the use of עול instead of עלילה. עול (the masculine to עולה), <hi type="italic">pravitas</hi>, is the accusative of the object (cf. <reference osisRef="Ezek.16.52">Eze 16:52</reference>) to both verbs, which give it a twofold superlative attributive notion. Moreover, here השׁחיתו is accented with <hi type="italic">Mugrash</hi> in our printed texts instead of <hi type="italic">Tarcha</hi>. One <hi type="italic">Mugrash</hi> after another is contrary to all rule.
entries.7c3e9b8130b51d63f99451fa6e0533b6c99d69af: <reference osisRef="Ps.53.2">Psa 53:2</reference> <div eID="gen9543" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9544" type="x-p"/> In both recensions of the Psalm the name of God occurs seven times. In <reference osisRef="Ps.14.1-Ps.14.7">Psa 14:1-7</reference> it reads three times <hi type="italic">Elohim</hi> and four times <hi type="italic">Jahve</hi>; in the Psalm before us it is all seven times <hi type="italic">Elohim</hi>, which in this instance is a proper name of equal dignity with the name <hi type="italic">Jahve</hi>. Since the mingling of the two names in <reference osisRef="Ps.14.1-Ps.14.7">Psa 14:1-7</reference> is perfectly intentional, inasmuch as <hi type="italic">Elohim</hi> in <reference osisRef="Ps.53.1">Psa 53:1</reference>, <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.53.2">Psa 53:2</reference></hi> describes God as a Being most highly exalted and to be reverentially acknowledged, and in <reference osisRef="Ps.52.5">Psa 52:5</reference> as the Being who is present among men in the righteous generation and who is mighty in their weakness, it becomes clear that David himself cannot be the author of this levelling change, which is carried out more rigidly than the Elohimic character of the Psalm really demands.
entries.7062b032adb4f8de1e0a61b06d094c582025f5a3: <reference osisRef="Ps.53.3">Psa 53:3</reference> <div eID="gen9544" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9545" type="x-p"/> Instead of הכּל, the totality, we have כּלּו, which denotes each individual of the whole, to which the suffix, that has almost vanished (<reference osisRef="Ps.29.9">Psa 29:9</reference>) from the genius of the language, refers. And instead of סר, the more elegant סג, without any distinction in the meaning.
entries.1428bcd691f89184bb3cfaf3f9d4b5ab11e4e889: <reference osisRef="Ps.53.4">Psa 53:4</reference> <div eID="gen9545" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9546" type="x-p"/> Here in the first line the word כּל־, which, as in <reference osisRef="Ps.5.6">Psa 5:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.6.9">Psa 6:9</reference>, is in its right place, is wanting. In <reference osisRef="Ps.14.1-Ps.14.7">Psa 14:1-7</reference> there then follow, instead of two tristichs, two distichs, which are perhaps each mutilated by the loss of a line. The writer who has retouched the Psalm has restored the tristichic symmetry that had been lost sight of, but he has adopted rather violent means: inasmuch as he has fused down the two distichs into a single tristich, which is as closely as possible adapted to the sound of their letters.
entries.dd6fe3ff6460b2805065dce5feb7bdaef780edfb: <reference osisRef="Ps.53.5">Psa 53:5</reference> <div eID="gen9546" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9547" type="x-p"/> The last two lines of this tristich are in letters so similar to the two distichs of <reference osisRef="Ps.14.1-Ps.14.7">Psa 14:1-7</reference>, that they look like an attempt at the restoration of some faded manuscript. Nevertheless, such a close following of the sound of the letters of the original, and such a changing of the same by means of an interchange of letters, is also to be found elsewhere (more especially in Jeremiah, and e.g., also in the relation of the Second Epistle of Peter to Jude). And the two lines sound so complete in themselves and full of life, that this way of accounting for their origin takes too low an estimate of them. A later poet, perhaps belonging to the time of Jehoshaphat or Hezekiah, has here adapted the Davidic Psalm to some terrible catastrophe that has just taken place, and given a special character to the universal announcement of judgment. The addition of לא־היה פּחד (supply אשׁר = אשׁר שׁם, <reference osisRef="Ps.84.4">Psa 84:4</reference>) is meant to imply that fear of judgment had seized upon the enemies of the people of God, when no fear, i.e., no outward ground for fear, existed; it was therefore חרדּת אלהים (<reference osisRef="1Sam.14.15">1Sa 14:15</reference>), a God-wrought panic. Such as the case with the host of the confederates in the days of Jehoshaphat (<reference osisRef="2Chr.20.22-2Chr.20.24">2Ch 20:22-24</reference>); such also with the army of Sennacherib before Jerusalem (<reference osisRef="Isa.37.36">Isa 37:36</reference>). כּי gives the proof in support of this fright from the working of the divine power. The words are addressed to the people of God: <hi type="italic">Elohim hath scattered the bones</hi> (so that unburied they lie like dirt upon the plain a prey to wild beasts, <reference osisRef="Ps.141.7">Psa 141:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.6.5">Eze 6:5</reference>) <hi type="italic">of thy besieger</hi>, i.e., of him who had encamped against thee. חנך .eeht tsniaga instead of חנך = חנה עליך.<note placement="foot">So it has been explained by Menachem; whereas Dunash wrongly takes the ך of חנך as part of the root, overlooking the fact that with the suffix it ought rather to have been חנך instead of חנך. It is true that within the province of the verb <hi type="italic">âch</hi> does occur as a pausal masculine suffix instead of <hi type="italic">écha</hi>, with the preterite (<reference osisRef="Deut.6.17">Deu 6:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.30.19">Isa 30:19</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.55.5">Isa 55:5</reference>, and even out of pause in <reference osisRef="Jer.23.37">Jer 23:37</reference>), and with the infinitive (<reference osisRef="Deut.28.24">Deu 28:24</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.28.15">Eze 28:15</reference>), but only in the passage before us with the participle. Attached to the participle this masculine suffix closely approximates to the Aramaic; with proper substantives there are no examples of it found in Hebrew. Simson ha-Nakdan, in his חבור הקונים (a MS in Leipzig University Library, fol. 29 <hi type="italic">b</hi>), correctly observes that forms like שׁמך, עמּך, are not biblical Hebrew, but Aramaic, and are only found in the language of the Talmud, formed by a mingling of the Hebrew and Aramaic.</note> <div eID="gen9547" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9548" type="x-p"/> By the might of his God, who has overthrown them, the enemies of His people, Israel has put them to shame, i.e., brought to nought in a way most shameful to them, the project of those who were so sure of victory, who imagined they could devour Israel as easily and comfortably as bread. It is clear that in this connection even <reference osisRef="Ps.53.5">Psa 53:5</reference> receives a reference to the foreign foes of Israel originally alien to the Psalm, so that consequently Mic 3:3 is no longer a parallel passage, but passages like Num 14:9, <hi type="italic">our bread are they</hi> (the inhabitants of Canaan); and <reference osisRef="Jer.30.16">Jer 30:16</reference>, <hi type="italic">all they that devour thee shall be devoured</hi>.
entries.915c38a3d65b6eb73d2c0dc50924c7d4bd4d8000: <reference osisRef="Ps.53.6">Psa 53:6</reference> <div eID="gen9548" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9549" type="x-p"/> The two texts now again coincide. Instead of ישׁוּעת, we here have ישׁעות; the expression is strengthened, the plural signifies entire, full, and final salvation. Consolation in the Presence of Bloodthirsty Adversaries (In the Hebrew, <reference osisRef="Ps.54.1-Ps.54.2">Psa 54:1-2</reference> comprise the designation 'To the leader, with the accompaniment of stringed instruments, a Maskil of David...'; from then on <reference osisRef="Ps.54.1-Ps.54.7">Psa 54:1-7</reference> in English translation corresponds to vv. 3-9 in the Hebrew) <div eID="gen9549" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9550" type="x-p"/> Here again we have one of the eight Psalms dates from the time of Saul’s persecution - a <hi type="italic">Maskı̂l</hi>, like the two preceding Psalms, and having points of close contact both with <reference osisRef="Ps.53.1-Ps.53.6">Psa 53:1-6</reference> (cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.54.5">Psa 54:5</reference> with <reference osisRef="Ps.53.3">Psa 53:3</reference>) and with <reference osisRef="Ps.52.1-Ps.52.9">Psa 52:1-9</reference> (cf. the resemblance in the closing words of. v. 8 and Ps 52:11): <hi type="italic">To the Precentor, with the accompaniment of stringed instruments</hi> (vid., on <reference osisRef="Ps.4.1">Psa 4:1</reference>), <hi type="italic">a meditation, by David, when the Ziphites came and said to Saul: Is not David hidden among us?</hi> Abiathar, the son of Ahimelech, had escaped to David, who with six hundred men was then in the fortified town of Keïla (Keilah), but received through Abiathar the divine answer, that the inhabitants would give him up if Saul should lay siege to the town. Thereupon we find him in the wilderness of Zîph; the Ziphites betray him and pledge themselves to capture him, and thereby he is in the greatest straits, out of which he was only rescued by an invasion of the Philistines, which compelled Saul to retreat (1Sa 23:19.). The same history which the earlier narrator of the Books of Samuel relates here, we meet with once more in 1 Sam. 26, related with fuller colouring. The form of the inscription of the Psalm is word for word the same as both in <reference osisRef="1Sam.23.19">1Sa 23:19</reference> and in <reference osisRef="1Sam.26.1">1Sa 26:1</reference>; the annals are in all three passages the ultimate source of the inscription.  <chapter eID="Ps.53"/> <div eID="gen9550" type="x-p"/>

entries.e1750815271c36af5b0154fd7b338b657f0737a8:
PSALM 53
This psalm being almost identical with the fourteenth, it has not been considered necessary to subjoin any distinct commentary.
Some slight differences will be found, on comparison, between this and the 14th psalm; the chief of which is in the 5th verse. For Calvin’s explanation of this verse, see volume 1, p. 199. It is not easy to say whether these variations are owing to transcribers, or whether they were made by some prophetic bard, who, during some afflictive period of Jewish history, adapted the 14th psalm, by a few alterations, to circumstances different from those for which it was originally composed. Theodoret is of this last opinion, and refers it to the alarm created by Sennacherib’s invasion under the reign of Hezekiah; others think it was written during the captivity — a conjecture which is founded on the last verse, “O that the salvation of Israel were come out of Zion!”
To the chief musician upon Mahalath.
What מהלת, mahalath, signifies, in the title of this and the 88th psalm, must be uncertain, the word not being found elsewhere. It is most probably the name of an instrument on which the psalm was to be sung; and it may fitly be deduced from חלל, perforavit, or incidit, either from the hollowness of the instrument, or farther, from the holes cut in it; in which respect חליל is ordinarily used for fistula, or tibia, a pipe.” — Hammond
A Psalm of David for instruction.
Psalm 53:1-6
1. The fool hath said in his heart, There is no God: they have become corrupt, they have done abominable works: there is none that doeth good. 2. God looked down from heaven upon the children of men, to see if there were any that did understand, that did seek God. 3. Every one of them has gone back; they have together become filthy: there is none that doeth good, no, not one. 4. Have the workers of iniquity no knowledge? eating my people as they eat bread:
“C’est, n’en font non plus de conscience, que de manger un morceau de pain.” — Fr. marg. “That is, they have no more scruple in doing this than in eating a morsel of bread.”
they have not called upon God. 5. There were they in great fear where no fear was; for God hath scattered the bones of him that encampeth against thee: thou hast put them to shame, because God hath despised them. 6. Who shall give the salvation of Israel out of Zion? When God bringeth back the captivity of his people,
“C’est, son peuple captif.” — Fr. marg. “That is, his captive people.”
Jacob shall rejoice, and Israel shall triumph.

                  <ns0:head>PSAL. LIII.</ns0:head>
                  <ns0:head>To the chief musician upon Mahalath <ns0:hi>a,</ns0:hi> Maschil, <ns0:hi>a Psalm</ns0:hi> of David.</ns0:head>
                  <ns0:argument>
                     <ns0:p>This <ns0:hi>Psalm</ns0:hi> some few Words excepted is wholly the same with <ns0:hi>Psal.</ns0:hi> 14. and therefore the Reader must resort thither for the Interpretation of it. And it is repeated; Partly, because the matter of it is so important and necessary to be known and considered; and Partly, because there arose some new and suitable Occasion, which made <ns0:hi>David</ns0:hi> sing it a second time, and that with some small Alterations. And the Com<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />piler or Compilers of <ns0:hi>David</ns0:hi>'s <ns0:hi>Psalms,</ns0:hi> had so great a Reve<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />rence for their Composer, whom they knew to be guided by divine Inspiration, that they would not lose any of his Fragments, and therefore repeated this <ns0:hi>Psalm</ns0:hi> with the Vari<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ations which he had made. <ns0:hi>a</ns0:hi> This also seems to be the Name of a musical Instrument, or Tune; Wherein, as in the rest of them, it is better to Confess our Ignorance, as the Hebrew Doctors themselves do, than to give way to Vain and groundless Conjectures about them.</ns0:p>
                  </ns0:argument>
                  <ns0:p n="1">1. THe <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Psal. 10. 4. & 14. 1. <ns0:hi>&c.</ns0:hi>
                     </ns0:note> fool hath said in his heart, <ns0:hi>There is</ns0:hi> no God: corrupt are they, and have done abominable iniquity: <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Rom. 3. 10.</ns0:note> 
                     <ns0:hi>there is</ns0:hi> none that doth good.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="2">2. God looked down from heaven upon the children of men, to see if there were <ns0:hi>any</ns0:hi> that did understand, that did seek God.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="3">3. Every one of them is gone back, they are altogether become filthy; <ns0:hi>there is</ns0:hi> none that doth good, no not one.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="4">4. Have the workers of iniquity no know<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ledge? who eat up my people <ns0:hi>as</ns0:hi> they eat bread; they have not called upon God.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="5">5. There <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> they <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                           <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>
                        <ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ed a Fear.</ns0:note> were they in great fear, <ns0:hi>where</ns0:hi> no fear was <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">(<ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi>) Where there was no great nor sufficient Cause of Fear, See <ns0:hi>Levit.</ns0:hi> 26. 36. <ns0:hi>Deut.</ns0:hi> 28. 65. <ns0:hi>Iob</ns0:hi> 15. 21. <ns0:hi>Prov.</ns0:hi> 28. 1. They who designed to secure themselves, from all Fear and Danger by their Contempt of God, and by the Persecution of good Men, and by other wicked Courses, were by those means filled with the Terrors which they sought to avoid.</ns0:note>: for God hath scattered the bones <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">Hath not onely broken their <ns0:hi>Bones, (i. e.</ns0:hi>) Their strength and force, which is oft noted by the Bones, as <ns0:hi>Psal.</ns0:hi> 6. 2. and 31. 10. and 51. 8. but also dispersed them hither and thither, so as there is no Hopes of a Re-union and Restauration.</ns0:note> of him that encampeth <ns0:hi>against</ns0:hi> thee <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">(<ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi>) A<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />gainst <ns0:hi>my People,</ns0:hi> expressed v. 4. or <ns0:hi>Israel,</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>Zion,</ns0:hi> as it is in the next Verse.</ns0:note>, thou <ns0:note n="e" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>Thou</ns0:hi> Oh <ns0:hi>Zion</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>Ierusalem,</ns0:hi> which they be<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />siege.</ns0:note> hast put <ns0:hi>them</ns0:hi> to shame <ns0:note n="f" place="bottom">For the great and strange disappointment of their Hopes and Confidence. It was a great Reproach to them, for such numerous and mighty Forces, to be baffled and Conquer<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ed by those whom they thought to swallow up at a Morsel.</ns0:note>, because God hath despised them <ns0:note n="g" place="bottom">Or, <ns0:hi>Rejected them,</ns0:hi> Cursed them. Therefore it is no wonder if they could not stand before thee.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="6">6. <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> who will give Salvations &c.</ns0:note> O that the salvation of Israel <ns0:hi>were come</ns0:hi> out of Zion, when God bringeth back the cap<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tivity of his people Jacob shall rejoyce, and Is<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />rael shall be glad.</ns0:p>
